658b2e56-b820-11f1-951d-f7f30964c274.recap: Henry Peabody of GMO discusses a paper on the Fed's unofficial 'third mandate': managing credit transmission across an increasingly debanked economy. He argues financial conditions remain easy for high-quality, termed-out corporate borrowers and AI-related capex, but tight for consumers and lower-quality credits (mortgages ~6%, auto loans north of 7%, triple-C clearing coupons above 10-12%). This bifurcation exists because non-bank lenders (private credit) don't tighten in response to Fed hikes the way regulated banks do, since their cost of capital isn't tied to deposits or bank balance-sheet constraints, and losses are less visible/transparent than in a banked system, making it hard to gauge where we are in the credit cycle. He expects rates to stay higher for longer until 'cracks form,' with triple-C spreads widening as a leading indicator of rising defaults, though not yet a spike. He flags software/IP-heavy private credit as vulnerable given poor recovery prospects (no hard assets). On positioning, GMO is underweight vanilla credit risk (IG, HY, EM beta) and duration, preferring short, seasoned, up-in-capital-structure structured product (AAA CLOs, student loans, non-agency MBS) for predictable, less-correlated returns. He's skeptical of yield-focused BDCs based on 2008-era experience (return of capital, cherry-picked portfolio sales). On rates, he favors the belly of the curve (3-5yr) as a hedge, expects further curve flattening, and sees long-end selling driven by real rates/term premium rather than pure inflation, tied to competition for capital from AI buildout and fiscal sustainability concerns (Social Security trust fund depletion in the mid-2030s).
terms: OIS -- Overnight Index Swap, a rate derivative referencing the average overnight rate over a period
CLO -- Collateralized Loan Obligation, a securitization backed by a pool of leveraged loans
BDC -- Business Development Company, a publicly or privately traded vehicle that lends to (often private) middle-market companies
NAV -- Net Asset Value, the per-share value of a fund's underlying assets
CDS -- Credit Default Swap, a derivative contract providing credit protection against an issuer's default

6ab4ca5362a47b6beca89783.one_liner: A broad-strokes HSBC macro podcast on Fed tightening and how Asian central banks (especially Japan, and by contrast mainland China) are responding, with a direct read-through to the HKD peg and HK rate sensitivity.
6ab4ca5362a47b6beca89783.recap: HSBC's Harald van der Linde and Fred Neumann discuss the Fed's latest hike, framed as hawkish given persistent inflation from rising energy (diesel) prices and a brewing El Niño threatening Asian food inflation. Markets are pricing further hikes since the Fed historically moves in multi-step cycles rather than one-off adjustments. Because the Fed sets the global price of money, most Asian central banks are following suit to avoid currency weakness feeding import-cost inflation: Japan's central bank hiked days after the Fed (unusual after decades of near-zero rates, driven by rising wages and food prices), with Australia, Korea, Indonesia, the Philippines and India also expected to tighten. Mainland China is the outlier, with disinflation/near-deflation and weak consumption/investment giving its central bank room to hold or even ease; capital controls insulate the renminbi from the usual divergence-driven outflow pressure, and HSBC's house view sees room for RMB strength on export surpluses. On equities, rising rates should pressure valuations, but AI-driven capex is generating order flow for Asian tech supply chains, complicating the picture. Hong Kong, due to its USD currency peg, is described as unusually rate-sensitive, and the hosts note a Hong Kong-versus-Shanghai listing arbitrage where the same mainland company can be priced differently due to capital-flow differences. The episode closes with a lighthearted forecast game: hosts predict India, Korea, Indonesia and Taiwan raise rates over six months, while China stays on hold.
